# Underestimation of Sector-Wide Methane Emissions from United States Wastewater Treatment

**Authors:** Daniel
P. Moore; Nathan P. Li; Lars P. Wendt; Sierra R. Castañeda; Mark M. Falinski; Jun-Jie Zhu; Cuihong Song; Zhiyong Jason Ren; Mark A. Zondlo

**Affiliations:** †Department of Civil & Environmental Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey08544, United States | ‡Now at Department of Earth Systems Science, Stanford University, Stanford, California94305, United States | §Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey08544, United States

## Abstract

An increasing percentage of US waste methane (CH4) emissions come from wastewater treatment (10% in 1990 to 14% in 2019), although there are limited measurements across the sector, leading to large uncertainties in current inventories. We conducted the largest study of CH4 emissions from US wastewater treatment, measuring 63 plants with average daily flows ranging from 4.2 × 10–4 to 8.5 m3 s–1 (<0.1 to 193 MGD), totaling 2% of the 62.5 billion gallons treated, nationally. We employed Bayesian inference to quantify facility-integrated emission rates with a mobile laboratory approach (1165 cross-plume transects). The median plant-averaged emission rate was 1.1 g CH4 s–1 (0.1–21.6 g CH4 s–1; 10th/90th percentiles; mean 7.9 g CH4 s–1), and the median emission factor was 3.4 × 10–2 g CH4 (g influent 5 day biochemical oxygen demand; BOD5)−1 [0.6–9.9 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1; 10th/90th percentiles; mean 5.7 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1]. Using a Monte Carlo-based scaling of measured emission factors, emissions from US centrally treated domestic wastewater are 1.9 (95% CI: 1.5–2.4) times greater than the current US EPA inventory (bias of 5.4 MMT CO2-eq). With increasing urbanization and centralized treatment, efforts to identify and mitigate CH4 emissions are needed.

## Abstract

The US EPA sector-wide methane emissions inventory is underestimated by a factor of 1.9 based on measurements from 63 treatment plants across the US.

## Introduction

Methane (CH4) is a potent greenhouse gas (GHG) with global warming potentials of 80–83 and 27–30 over 20 and 100 years’ time horizons, respectively.1 Due to the relatively short atmospheric lifetime of CH4 (∼9 years),2 rapid mitigation efforts will yield near-term results in combatting increased radiative forcing and warming. Despite this, CH4 emissions continue to increase, and the waste industry (including solid and liquid waste management) is the third-largest contributor (∼15%) of global non-CO2 GHG emissions, behind only the agriculture and energy sectors.3 Further, centralized wastewater treatment is expanding globally in response to a growing and increasingly urbanized population, leading to a rise in CH4 emissions from these facilities. This makes understanding and mitigating CH4 emissions from wastewater treatment an increasingly urgent need.

According to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA),4 centralized domestic wastewater treatment in the US, including anaerobic sludge digestion, is responsible for 250 kt CH4 (6.3 MMT CO2-eq), or roughly 14% of waste CH4 emissions (1% of national anthropogenic CH4 emissions). This is driven by the by-production of CH4 via the microbial breakdown of organic waste during wastewater and sludge treatment processes under anaerobic conditions.5,6 Guidelines developed by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) estimate CH4 emissions from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) using plant-specific treatment processes, sludge handling, and discharge methods.7 However, these guidelines were developed from previous monitoring studies using a range of measurement techniques focused on one or few facilities,8−12 with a particular focus on Europe,9,12−16 China,10,17 Mexico,18,19 and the US,8,20 calling into question their representativeness across the sector in different countries. Previously measured emission factors (EFs), which are often defined as emission rates (ERs) normalized by organic loading, range several orders of magnitude from 6.2 × 10–4 g CH4 (g 5 day biochemical oxygen demand, BOD5)−1 to 6.4 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1. This large variability may be a result of differences in influent conditions, plant-specific treatment processes and/or operating conditions, or systematic biases from particular measurement techniques, and likely propagates to the current national-scale inventories.

Most early quantification efforts of WWTP emissions utilized bottom-up gas and water sampling.8,10 Bottom-up, process-level studies focus on a specific location and small magnitude of emissions from individual sources, so they may not resolve large-scope facility-integrated emissions or unknown sources, such as leaks,9,21 unintended anaerobic processes, and/or significant incomplete combustion of biogas produced in the system. Omission of such sources inherently leads to biases and underestimations in emissions from the full treatment process. Contrastingly, assuming homogeneity of emissions from a source when measuring only a subset or portion of it may lead to overestimations.22,23 As a result, more recent studies utilize top-down, mobile-based remote-sensing techniques.9,13,14,16 The primary advantage of top-down methodologies is the ability to quantify facility-integrated emissions. For instance, by using a top-down, mobile-based method via tracer release,8,15,18,21 Delre et al.14 found that a leak in an anaerobic digester, which otherwise would likely have been neglected by component-wise measurements, increased the facility CH4 emissions 3-fold compared to when the leak was fixed. Indeed, facility-integrated emissions have been found to be up to 10 times greater than component-wise measurements.9,24 However, the site access and labor requirements associated with tracer release restrict the ability to efficiently analyze many plants to capture a representative sample of facilities in the country across locations, sizes, and treatment types.

In this study, we measured CH4 emissions and quantified associated uncertainties from 63 WWTPs in the US using mobile laboratory-based measurements with inverse Gaussian dispersion modeling and Bayesian source rate inference. The relatively large number of WWTPs allows for a better understanding of the magnitude and variability of wastewater treatment emissions in the US. Gaussian dispersion modeling is an alternative top-down approach to quantify plant-scale emissions, which has proven effective in estimating trace gas emissions from single-point,25,26 multi-point,27,28 and area sources.29,30 This approach requires less equipment, site access, and labor compared to other top-down methods (e.g., tracer release), allowing for more rapid data acquisition. Although uncertainties associated with atmospheric variability and dispersion coefficients for an individual observation can be larger than with a tracer release,27 by averaging many sites across a range of atmospheric conditions, we can compile a more representative estimate of wastewater CH4 emissions, which can be used to improve the current understanding of emissions from this sector. Further, current inventories are based on guidelines that use measurements from only 14 WWTPs and calculate emissions from each treatment step (i.e., wastewater, solids, and discharge) individually and later aggregate them to a facility-integrated value. Results from the current study are presented in the context of plant-specific estimates using these guidelines and expand the data set used to inform them.

## Materials and Methods

### Sampling Methods

We measured CH4 with an LI-7700 (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA), an open-path, high frequency (5–10 Hz) sensor, mounted on the Princeton Atmospheric Chemistry Experiment (PACE) Mobile Laboratory,31,32 an electric vehicle-based mobile laboratory designed to avoid sampling self-emissions. Carbon monoxide (CO) concentrations for traffic-based combustion interference were measured using a custom open-path, quantum cascade laser-based sensor operating at 10 Hz.33,34 The use of open-path sensors for mobile quantification of emissions avoids the difficulties associated with slower response time instruments and sampling manifolds.35 Concurrent meteorological data (i.e., wind speed and direction, temperature) were recorded using an Airmar WX200 (Airmar, Milford, NH, USA), and data were geo-located using a 1–10Hz GPS (Garmin, Olathe, KS, USA). Section S1 in the Supporting Information provides a more detailed description of the accuracy and precision of the instruments used, in addition to the wind statistics, which were calculated using a combination of in situ measurements and reanalysis data.

The source inversion technique employed in this study, and further discussed in the following section, requires sampling the entire plume such that background CH4 concentration levels are reached on either side of the enhancement. Forecasted meteorological conditions were used to inform route planning by determining probable plume locations. CH4 concentrations were monitored in real time to ensure traversal of the full plume. In addition, for each observational period at a WWTP, we targeted at least 10 individual transects of the plume. Instantaneous plumes are stochastic in nature, and prior modeling and observational work has shown that performing 10 traverses maintains the efficiency of mobile sampling while minimizing the stochastic effects of turbulence.27

### Integrated Gaussian Plume Dispersion Approach

We employed a Gaussian dispersion model with total reflection at the surface36 to represent the CH4 enhancements (above background) downwind of a point source (Section S2). As described by Albertson et al.,37 cross-plume integration minimizes the uncertainty due to crosswind turbulent variability. Therefore, integrations of both the modeled and measured plumes were used to infer source rates for each observational period. As discussed in Section S3, two screening measures and five quality control steps were taken to ensure that the data was valid for emission calculations using this method. Although 10 transects were targeted, due to sampling constraints and data quality control measures, 78% of observational periods utilized 10+ transects, 13% utilized 7–9 transects, and 9% utilized 2–6 transects (though with greater uncertainty).

The modeled source was chosen based on satellite imagery. Where applicable, locations of anaerobic digesters were chosen to be the point source for the model as they are the most likely source of CH4 emissions from WWTPs.11 When multiple digesters were located at the facility, a location central to the appropriate structures was chosen. A point source was defined as the geometric center of facilities without anaerobic digesters. Although this method of choosing a point source location is likely to introduce biases on an individual plant basis, the average across many sites will converge as the actual source locations should be randomly distributed with respect to the centroid. There is uncertainty associated with assuming a point source from these plants, which are likely a combination of point and area sources both known and unknown (i.e., leaks) to the plant operators. However, without further knowledge of, or access to, each site, multi-point or area source models cannot be used. For a further discussion regarding the use and validation of this method, the reader is referred to Section S4.

### Bayesian Inference

Although we employed an integrated Gaussian dispersion model approach, a Bayesian framework in conjunction with inverse dispersion modeling, similar to that described by Zhou et al.,38 incorporates uncertainties of both the observations and model inputs to robustly calculate ERs and their overall uncertainty. ### Site Descriptions

63 WWTPs located in the mid-Atlantic region and California were sampled from July 2019 through November 2021. Sites were chosen to encompass a wide range of treatment types and flow rates. The sampled 63 WWTPs span the typical treatment processes representative of plants in the US. We categorized them into three groups: plants with anaerobic digestion (AD;1) and without AD (2) that employ centralized aerobic wastewater treatment and (3) plants that treat wastewater using anaerobic reactors/lagoons. Detailed treatment processes of the sampled 63 plants, which are listed in Table S4, were collected by analyzing publicly available data and emailing plant officials. Despite these efforts, specific treatment processes for the sampled plants were incomplete and possibly out of date. The average daily flow for the studied plants (2020–2021) ranges 4 orders of magnitude from 0.01 to 193 million gallons per day (MGD; 4.2 × 10–4 to 8.5 m3 s–1). The 63 sampled WWTPs treat a combined average of 1332 MGD or about 2% of the 62 500 MGD treated by centralized domestic wastewater facilities in the US, according to the American Society of Civil Engineers.39 For the discussion below, we will often refer to the size categories as defined by the US EPA, where small, medium, and large plants are defined by average flows of <1 MGD (<0.04 m3 s–1), 1–10 MGD (0.04–0.4 m3 s–1), and >10 MGD (>0.4 m3 s–1), respectively. Sampled plants exhibit a similar size distribution compared to all US plants, with a slight bias toward higher flow facilities when considering the total sampled flow (Figure S15). Of the 63 plants in the current study, 49 reported monthly influent data including flow and BOD5 (Table S5).

## Results and Discussion

### Observations of CH4 Plumes

We analyzed a total of 95 observational periods for the 63 unique WWTPs as 20 plants were sampled multiple times. Each observational period consisted of at least 2 and up to 32 transects. In total, 1,165 transects of instantaneous CH4 plumes from the WWTPs passed quality control. Most measurements were captured during daylight hours, and all measurements were taken between 06:49 and 22:54 local time across a range of atmospheric and sampling conditions (Table S6).

Figure 1a shows an example of an observational period where measurements were captured across 11 transects of the CH4 plume along the north path. The stochastic nature of plume dispersion is evident by the variability in the instantaneous plume width and magnitude and peak location. A representative example of transect-averaged results is shown in Figure 1c, which shows the averaged concentration measurements from 11 transects, each, for the two routes downwind of the plant separated by ∼25 meters. This site provides an opportunity to investigate the effect of downwind distance (i.e., turbulent dispersion) on the quantification method. While Figure 1a exhibits a significant variability in enhancement magnitude and location for the northern (further) downwind transects, averaging the concentration values across all transects results in a more Gaussian plume structure, as seen in Figure 1c. As expected, the enhancements along the further transects are significantly lower in magnitude than the nearer transects and exhibit a broader plume due to turbulent diffusion. The far transect peak concentration (4.2 ppmv) is 55% lower than that of the near transect (9.4 ppmv), and the plume widths of the far and near transects, defined as the distance between the 10th percentiles of the enhancements, are 703 and 266 meters, respectively. The point-source assumption, as discussed in Section 2.2, results in a narrower modeled plume compared to the observations (Figure 1c); however, the quantification methods incorporate uncertainty with regard to the true source location and configuration (see Section S5). The integrated plume approach with data from either the near or the far transects alone elicits agreeable emission estimates for this observational period [4.8 (1.7–8.1) g CH4 s–1 and 4.5 (1.9–7.4) g CH4 s–1, respectively; 4.2 (2.1–6.5) g CH4 s–1 combined, Figure 1b; all values represent the mean (10th/90th percentile) emission rate].

The PDF measured after the first transect processed using an initial uninformative uniform prior distribution is shown as a dotted black line in (b). ### Observed Emission Rates

In the context of the Bayesian framework described in Section 2.3 (and further in Section S5), the initial prior PDF is uninformative (i.e., uniform), which can result in broad posterior PDFs after processing just one transect. Beyond the first transect, however, the posterior PDF of the previous transect defines the prior distribution, and with each subsequent transect processed, the posterior PDF, from which the ER and associated uncertainty are calculated, converges (Figure 1b). For instance, the average relative variance after processing the final transect for each observational period is 0.20 (see Section S6 for a detailed discussion of the posterior PDF convergence). Measured ERs for each observational period were then determined as the expected value of the final posterior PDF. A summary of estimated emissions and associated uncertainties are given in Table S6 and presented graphically in Figure 2a. The error term in the Bayesian source rate estimation method was largely driven by the atmospheric dispersion model uncertainty.

*Figure 2: Estimated CH4 emission rate (a) and emission factor (b; emission rate normalized by influent organic load, where available) for plants with different flow rates, averaged across observational periods, where applicable. Colors/markers indicate the type of treatment used by each plant. The best fit line, as determined by orthogonal distance regression on a log–log plot, is given in (a) and the log-linear relationship between ER and flow rate (F; slope of 1.2 ± 0.1, intercept of 1.0 ± 0.1) is given. Error bars represent the standard deviation around the mean. Both axes are presented on a log scale.*

Overall, the final emissions estimated using the Bayesian framework, which considers background variability, were above the detection limit (see Section S5) for 84% of transects (980 of 1,165) with the median (10th/90th percentile) detection limit across all 1,165 transects being 0.3 (0.1–1.9) g CH4 s–1 (mean, 0.8 g CH4 s–1). Measured ERs for all observational periods from all sites span roughly 4 orders of magnitude, from 0.01 to 74.8 g CH4 s–1 with a plant-averaged median (10th/90th percentile) emission of 1.1 (0.1–21.6) g CH4 s–1 (mean, 7.9 g CH4 s–1), which agrees well with previous measurements that range from 0.01 to 33.3 g CH4 s–1.8,13

Out of the 63 plants sampled, 43 were sampled once, 15 were sampled twice, 3 were sampled thrice, 1 was sampled five times, and 1 was sampled eight times (Table S6). Measured ERs from plants sampled more than once were, on average, within a factor of 1.6 of the plant-averaged ER, and all were within a factor of 3.7 across ranges of temperatures, wind speeds, and direction (Figure S16). Thus, replicative sampling reveals generally consistent emissions from these plants and suggests minor day-to-day variability in CH4 emissions. Previous mobile analyses show similar variability between observations of the same plant. For instance, Delre et al.14 found “little variation” in emissions between observations with two important exceptions with clear causation. Additionally, Yoshida et al.13 estimated emissions from one treatment plant over 9 sampling periods, calculating emissions ranging a factor of 24. However, when at least 10 transects were measured and averaged over a given observational period, emissions were within a factor of 2.3 from the plant-averaged ER (Table 2 in ref (13)). This highlights the importance of replicative sampling to determine representative plant-scale emissions.

Figure 2a shows that a significant positive correlation (R2 = 0.55, p < 0.001) exists between the logarithm of the plant influent flow and the logarithm of the measured emission rate, determined using orthogonal distance regression. Emission rates gradually increased from 0.1 g CH4 s–1 for plants treating <0.1 MGD wastewater to 46 g CH4 s–1 for larger facilities that have a flow rate of >100 MGD. Most monitored plants are in the 1–10 MGD range, and CH4 emission rates from these plants are between 0.02 and 12.8 g CH4 s–1. This correlation is understandable as larger plants process larger amounts of organic matter. Finally, while Figure 2 highlights the basic treatment category used at the sampled facilities, we caution that there is a lack of data to draw significant conclusions based on the relationship between treatment and facility-integrated emissions.

### Emission Factors

Most previous works have attributed large variability in WWTP CH4 emissions to differences in treatment processes, infrastructure, and organic loading.10,11 Therefore, to better analyze our results across a wide range of influent organic loadings, we calculated the emission factors (EFs) as ERs normalized by influent BOD5 loading (Figure 2b; 2020–2021 means are given in Table S5). Monthly averages of influent BOD5 concentration for the month during which each observational period took place were used, and uncertainty was calculated as the standard deviation of monthly values over the year prior to the observational period. The following assumption was made in converting reported ERs to EFs with respect to BOD5:1.2 g BOD5 (g carbonaceous BOD; CBOD)−1.40 Plants lacking publicly available monthly influent BOD5 concentrations (14 of 63 plants) are not considered in Figure 2b and the associated EF analyses.

We analyzed an unprecedented range of plant sizes and found no clear trend in EFs among the plants with different capacities (Figure 2b). Specifically, no significant difference (Mann–Whitney nonparametric test, p = 0.31) in EFs from small- and medium-sized [median, 3.3 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1] and large WWTPs [median, 3.8 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1] was found. This supports the notion that influent organic content, regardless of size, is generally a good proxy for CH4 emissions. Further, plant-averaged EFs vary from 1.0 × 10–3 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1 to 0.4 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1 across all plants with different flows, though small (<1 MGD) plants demonstrated much larger variations [s.d. = 0.1 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1] than medium and large (>1 MGD) plants [s.d. = 0.03 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1]. The median (10th/90th percentile) EF across all plants is 3.4 (0.6–9.9) × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1 [mean, 5.7 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1]. Overall, our results support the large variability in plant-to-plant emissions observed in the literature.

As recognized by many studies, the actual EFs are influenced by various factors, so one should take the average number as a rough estimate but consider the plant specificity when estimating the CH4 emissions for any given plant. In particular, flow variability may alter individual estimations using this method as daily and sub-daily flow can range quite significantly,11 especially for utilities with shorter collection systems and travel times. Additionally, WWTPs with combined sewer lines and those with a greater proportion of industrial waste will experience significantly different influent statistics (e.g., flow rate and BOD5). Variability due to instantaneous differences in flow was not explicitly handled in our estimation as it was assumed to be negligible compared to other uncertainties.

Many previous top-down measurements have focused on plants with on-site AD, and results from the current study demonstrate a median EF of 3.4 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1 from these facilities, which agrees with the previous work (range 2.3 × 10–2 to 6.4 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1).12,14 However, previous plant-integrated mobile measurements of WWTPs with AD have not analyzed plants below 8 MGD. Of the 21 plants with digestion and reported influent data, the 9 with capacities <8 MGD exhibited significant overlap in measured EFs [median: 2.9 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1; 10th/90th percentile: 1.1 × 10–2 to 7.2 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1] compared with those >8 MGD [median: 3.6 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1; 10th/90th percentile: 0.8 × 10–2 to 8.6 × 10–2 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1]. Given that ∼95% of plants in the US operate <8 MGD, the relationship between EFs, treatment capacity, and treatment type is crucial to understanding the emissions across the sector.

### Scaling Emissions to the National Scale

The EPA inventory estimates that 6.3 million metric tons (MMT) of CO2-eq CH4 was emitted in the US in 2019 by a combination of centralized aerobic and anaerobic wastewater treatment, AD, and wastewater effluent, and a further 5.8 MMT CO2-eq was emitted from septic systems (not studied here).4 We employed a Monte Carlo analysis to scale measured emissions to the national level and directly compare to the EPA inventory. A full description of the methods used is given in Section S7. In short, we categorized the plants as small, medium, and large, as classified by the EPA, corresponding to <1 MGD (>0.04 m3 s–1), 1–10 MGD (0.04–0.4 m3 s–1), and >10 MGD (>0.4 m3 s–1), respectively. Assuming that the measured EF and associated uncertainty for each plant are equally representative across each category, we employed bootstrapping using the mean and standard deviations of the measured EFs to build a distribution for each size category. Thus, the magnitude and variability in measured EFs for each category, as discussed in Section 3.3, directly drive the scaled emissions for all plants of that size, nationally. A Monte Carlo approach was then applied to quantify the emissions by randomly selecting values from the distributions of each category, multiplying by the amount of waste treated by that category, and finally summing the emissions into a combined sector-wide emission.

Figure 3 shows the distribution of resulting national-scale emissions, as determined by the Monte Carlo analysis, compared to the current inventory. By calculating the expected value (mean) of the resulting lognormal distribution (green vertical line), we found that emissions from centrally treated domestic wastewater in the US are 11.6 (95% CI: 9.2–14.8) MMT CO2-eq yr–1, or a factor of 1.9 (95% CI: 1.5–2.4) greater than the current EPA inventory. For context, the current EPA inventory of 6.3 MMT CO2-eq yr–1 corresponds to the mode of the resulting distribution. This suggests an increase of the sector-wide emissions (including septic systems) to 17.4 MMT CO2-eq, or 2.5% of all US anthropogenic CH4 emissions (currently 1.8%). An alternative approach using a regression analysis between measured and estimated emissions yields similar results (see Section S8).

*Figure 3: Distribution of US emissions from domestic wastewater treatment, excluding septic systems. For reference, the expected value (mean) of the lognormal distribution (vertical green solid line) and the current US EPA inventory (vertical dotted black line) are shown.*

### Comparison to IPCC/EPA-Based EFs

While measured EFs showed no correlation with plant size, an alternative approach to investigating this relationship is to compare measured emissions to those estimated using IPCC guidelines, which serve as the basis for the current national EPA inventory. Following these guidelines (Section S9), emissions are estimated from each wastewater line, sludge line, and discharge according to plant-specific data and subsequently aggregated to estimate facility-integrated emissions. Uncertainty for each estimation is based on the range of monthly values for each relevant parameter. A default value of 250 mg BOD5 L–1 (±30%) was used for plants without reported BOD5 data and is greater than the proposed “medium strength” value for untreated domestic wastewater (190 mg L–1).41 This value was used as a conservative estimate as it is near the 75th percentile of known BOD5 values from the sampled plants. Using a Monte Carlo approach to incorporate the levels of uncertainty inherent in the IPCC’s methodology, resulting EFs for the sampled plants ranged from 0.005 to 0.05 g CH4 (g BOD5)−1. Overall, measured EFs from 71% of sampled plants were greater than the upper limit of IPCC-recommended EFs for the dominant US treatment type (centralized aerobic, Section S9).

We calculated the ratios between measured emissions and IPCC-based estimates (Section S10), which are displayed in Figure 4. The median (10th/90th percentile) ratio from the 63 sampled WWTPs is 2.9 (0.6–12.7). Moreover, the median ratio from treatment plants with AD (n = 28) is 3.2. In a bottom-up study, Daelman et al.11 showed that roughly 75% of plant-integrated emissions were from the anaerobic digesters. These suggest that IPCC methods, which fail to provide a clear guidance on aerobic treatment plants with on-site AD,18,19 overestimate the efficiency of these systems in terms of fugitive emissions.

*Figure 4: Ratio of measured CH4 emissions to IPCC-based estimates for 63 domestic wastewater treatment plants plotted by flow rate (MGD). Both axes are plotted on a logarithmic scale. Colors/markers indicate the type of treatment used by each plant. Values lying above the one-to-one line (black dotted horizontal line) are shaded blue, representing measurements that are greater than IPCC-based estimates. Conversely, values lying below the one-to-one line are shaded orange, suggesting that true emissions are overestimated when using the IPCC guidelines. The median ratio of 2.9 across all measured sites is presented (red line). For clarity, error bars in the x-direction are omitted.*

Figure 4 also suggests that IPCC guidelines disproportionally underestimate emissions from small- and medium-sized plants. Specifically, the median ratio of measured to estimated emissions for plants with an average daily flow of <10 MGD, which represent ∼97% of plants in the US,42 is 3.2. In contrast, the median ratio for large plants (>10 MGD) is 2.5, suggesting that the IPCC guidelines not only underestimate the large plants but also are especially unrepresentative of small- and medium-sized facilities.

## Implications and Future Work

We have presented the largest study of CH4 emission measurements of WWTPs by the number of sites and treatment types sampled for ER inter-comparison. We measured ERs, normalized EFs, and associated uncertainties from 63 WWTPs in the mid-Atlantic and California. These plants were sampled across 95 observational periods over a range of atmospheric conditions. We found that estimates based on the IPCC guidelines underestimate emissions from most WWTPs measured in the current study, especially those with lower daily influent flow. Based on the actual monitoring across the 63 plants of different sizes, the true CH4 emissions are 1.9 times higher than IPCC/EPA estimates, equating to a 5.1 MMT CO2-eq low bias in current inventories,4 if our results are representative. The Monte Carlo scaling revealed a highly skewed distribution, which has also been seen in other industries (e.g., gas and oil43) and is caused by the existence of a few large emitters. In the case of wastewater treatment, this is understandable given the similarly skewed distribution of US WWTP throughput.

Evidence from facilities that were sampled multiple times in the current study revealed no relationship between emissions and environmental variables, such as wind speed and direction, temperature, season, and time of day. Previous research11,44 has shown the existence of a diurnal pattern in CH4 emissions coinciding with influent flow and/or storage of dewatered solids, with a general increase in emissions during the morning, daytime maxima, and early morning minima. Therefore, more work is needed to quantify the timing and magnitude of diurnal patterns in CH4 emissions from WWTPs, but we acknowledge that the presented measurements exhibit a daytime bias (Figure S17) that we do not correct. We expect this bias to be highly plant specific based on influent flow characteristics, wastewater/solid residence times, and treatment practices, among other things, and it therefore needs more investigation.

As global population and urbanization rates rise, the environmental impacts of waste and wastewater treatment will become increasingly important. Our findings suggest that IPCC-based estimates underestimate CH4 emissions across all sizes of WWTPs, especially those with AD. The US EPA categorizes WWTPs as small (<1 MGD), medium (1–10 MGD), and large (>10 MGD), and although medium and large plants make up approximately 20% of the plants in the US and serve 89% of the nation’s population served by centralized treatment,42 the effect of plant size on CH4 emissions has not been robustly studied previous to this.

Our mobile sensing approach provides a rigorous and convenient method for large-scale monitoring of WWTP GHG emissions. In addition, our method allows us to sample many plants to gain a more representative sample size while averaging out biases associated with source location errors at individual plants. The current methodology provides a framework to measure many plants efficiently, often several in a day, which is useful for examining emissions from a range of treatment processes observed in the US.

This study presents CH4 emissions from plants that represent approximately 2% of centrally treated wastewater in the US. The number of facilities measured (63) is more than four times the number used to develop current IPCC-based guidelines for predicting emissions (14). The current CH4 emissions inventory is significantly underestimated, and additional data from plant operators of the sampled utilities, such as existing treatment processes and daily loading, can lead to the development of measurement-informed EFs, by treatment type, which may be used to update the existing IPCC guidelines and inform more accurate emission inventories. Despite gathering all publicly available data, process-level data were incomplete and/or out of date, and efforts to obtain this information are ongoing. Although this study provides the largest and most comprehensive analysis of wastewater CH4 emissions with regard to the range of WWTP sizes (i.e., average flow rates) and treatment types, it is still limited with regard to intensive analyses of specific treatment processes, geographic diversity, and seasonal and diurnal dependences. Therefore, further investigation is needed to develop robust sector-wide emission inventories considering all relevant variability.
